terms.definition: A triangle containing one 90° angle.
Either side forming the right angle of a right triangle.
The side opposite the right angle; the longest side of a right triangle.
For a right triangle with legs a,b and hypotenuse c, a²+b²=c².
A statement formed by reversing the hypothesis and conclusion of another statement; the Pythagorean converse can prove a triangle is right.
A value kept in symbolic form, such as 7√2, rather than rounded to a decimal.
An isosceles right triangle with side ratio 1:1:√2.
A special right triangle with side ratio 1:√3:2 opposite 30°,60°,90° respectively.
In a 30-60-90 triangle, the side opposite 30°.
In a 30-60-90 triangle, the side opposite 60°; √3 times the short leg.
A perpendicular segment from the right-angle vertex to the hypotenuse.
For positive a and b, √(ab); in right-triangle altitude relationships it links similar-triangle segments.
The segment of the hypotenuse associated with a leg in the right-triangle altitude theorem.
The chosen acute angle used to name opposite and adjacent sides.
The side across from the chosen reference angle.
The non-hypotenuse side touching the chosen reference angle.
For an acute angle in a right triangle, opposite divided by hypotenuse.
For an acute angle in a right triangle, adjacent divided by hypotenuse.
For an acute angle in a right triangle, opposite divided by adjacent.
Inverse sine, cosine, or tangent used to recover an angle from a side ratio.
Calculator angle setting required when answers are expected in degrees.
An angle measured upward from a horizontal reference line to a line of sight.
An angle measured downward from a horizontal reference line to a line of sight.
The straight line from an observer to the observed object.
A direction expressed from a reference direction, often north or south toward east or west.
A bearing such as N 35° E that starts from north or south and turns toward east or west.
A quantity with magnitude and direction.
The horizontal or vertical part of a vector.
The single vector equivalent to the combined effect of multiple vectors.
The directed change from a starting position to an ending position.
The length or size of a vector.
Difference between a measured or modeled value and the actual value, caused by instrument, setup, reading, or rounding limitations.
